html:
It matters a great deal, whether in China or abroad, and not only in academia. Here are a few examples.

My PhD offer. At a PhD fair in Beijing that year, I met two faculty members from Delft in the Netherlands and made a fairly good impression on them. After they got back, they introduced me to a professor. Unfortunately, he had already retired from Delft, so he introduced me to a research institute in Germany, and its professor became my PhD supervisor.

My postdoc offer. When I was applying for PhDs, this professor had also made me an offer, which I turned down when I went to Germany. Academia is a small world, especially in a niche field like ours. The first time I ran into him at a conference after starting my PhD, I didn’t dare go up and talk to him. The second time, I apologized to him sincerely. He said he had been very angry at first, but he understood. Later we met again at another conference, and so he got to know my face. Before the formal postdoc application process began, I got in touch with him; we were both happy with how things looked, so the application was just a formality. He then offered me a choice of two positions, and I picked one. Alas, after a year as a postdoc I left for industry, so now I need to find the next conference and apologize to him all over again...

My offer at my current company. At a conference in my third year as a PhD student, my supervisor introduced me to the CTO of the company I now work for. We kept running into each other at conferences after that and always chatted a bit. Before leaving my postdoc, I contacted the CTO and told him I wanted to move into industry. At the time the company was hiring a sales manager. After talking with him and the boss, we found we liked each other, and I got an offer as a scientist.

In none of these three stories did anyone ask who my dad was or whether my family was loaded. These are purer, simpler connections. Come prepared, meet lots of people, show you’re sincere, add a little bit of ability, and building a network, at least in European academia, isn’t hard. PhD life is fairly cut off, and the most important way to build a network is to go to conferences, especially international ones. Your own presentation, or other people’s, isn’t all that important. Some people take it far too seriously and neglect socializing, the most valuable thing a conference has to offer. I used to reassure a Chilean colleague at our institute who got nervous every time he gave a talk: “What you present, no one cares.” Sure enough, after that he stopped getting nervous. Give the academic content of a conference its due respect, and spend the rest of the time going and chatting with people!
